title: Three variables, two frameworks: the map before the journey
hook:
Pull up a long chart of the Nifty and squint. Blur out the quarterly results, the promoter scandals and the sector fads, and what's left is a market that rises and falls in a few big, shared waves. Inside those waves almost everything moves together, well-run companies and badly run ones alike.

Here's the thing: most of those waves come from just three forces. The price of oil. The price of money in America, which shows up as US real yields and the strength of the dollar. And the steady monthly pace at which Indians themselves put money into the market. The first two are set far away, in Gulf oil ministries and in a committee room at the Federal Reserve. The third is built at home, one salary-day SIP at a time.

This course is about how each of those forces reaches an Indian share price, which corners of the market each one hits, and what happens when they gang up. This first chapter is the map: why there are two frameworks, an Indian one and a global one, how they fit together, and how to use this page without reading it front to back.
short: Strip out company news and most of the shared movement in Indian stocks traces back to three variables: oil, US real yields and the dollar, and domestic flows.
Oil and US rates arrive from outside India; domestic flows are built at home. That split is why the course has an India framework and a global framework, joined by a short synthesis.
The variables matter most in combination. One going wrong usually means a correction, two at once means a proper drawdown, and domestic flows decide how deep it goes.
Right now two of the three are adverse at the same time, and domestic money is the buffer holding the market up.
Start with the chapter that explains the variable you understand least. Every chapter ends with where things stand today and what would change the call.

sections.heading: Why most of the market moves together
sections.html:
A stock moves on company news, sector news and whatever the whole market is doing. Over a year, for most large companies, the market's tide does a surprising share of the work. A professional calls it the market factor. You can call it the weather.

So what drives the weather? Go back to how a stock is priced. A share is worth the profits it will earn, multiplied by how much investors will pay for each rupee of those profits, the price-to-earnings multiple. Anything that moves the whole market has to move the earnings, move the multiple, or change who is doing the buying.

Now map the three variables onto that. Oil mostly hits earnings and inflation: it raises costs across a huge swathe of Indian companies and, through inflation, pushes the RBI towards higher rates. US real yields and the dollar mostly hit the multiple: they set the return a global investor can earn without taking any risk, and every Indian stock has to beat that to earn its place. Domestic flows decide the marginal buyer: when foreigners sell, is anyone at home ready to take the other side, and at what price?

Earnings, the multiple and the marginal buyer. Oil leans on the first, US rates on the second, domestic flows on the third.

Elections, monsoons and border clashes matter too, and each gets its own chapter. But in the big drawdowns of the past decade, at least one of these three is almost always at the centre.

And they are not independent. An oil spike raises American inflation too, which can push US yields up. A strong dollar usually comes with tighter money worldwide. Foreign selling is often a response to both. Half the skill in reading macro is noticing when the variables start pulling the same way.

sections.heading: Oil: the bill India pays in dollars
sections.html:
India imports most of the crude oil it uses, and pays for it in dollars. That makes oil the oldest source of macro stress in Indian markets, through a five-step chain.

First, the import bill swells. India already buys more from the world than it sells, a gap called the current account deficit, and a pricier barrel widens it almost mechanically. Second, more dollars are needed than are coming in, so the rupee weakens. Third, a weaker rupee makes every import dearer, not just oil, so inflation creeps up. Fourth, the RBI raises rates or tightens liquidity to defend the rupee and cap inflation. Fifth, higher rates lower the multiple the market will pay for earnings.

Oil also goes straight to profits. Paint makers, tyre companies, airlines and chemical firms all burn or process crude. State-run fuel retailers get squeezed when pump prices are held down, and if the government cuts fuel taxes instead, the money comes out of its own budget.

Who wins? Upstream oil and gas producers, whose realisations rise with the global price, and to a degree exporters, who gain from a weaker rupee. But for India as a whole, oil is a tax paid to the rest of the world, and the market treats it that way. The India chapter on oil and the rupee walks the twin-deficit chain in detail; the global chapter on oil and the Gulf explains who sets the price and why war premiums appear and vanish so fast.

sections.heading: US yields and the dollar: the world's price of money
sections.html:
The US ten-year Treasury yield is what the American government pays to borrow for ten years. Because that government is treated as the safest borrower on earth, its yield is the global benchmark for a risk-free return. Every other investment, including an Indian stock, is implicitly measured against it.

The real yield is that return after stripping out expected inflation. It tells a fund manager how much purchasing power they gain by doing nothing risky at all. When US real yields sit near zero, global investors go hunting for growth in places like India. When they rise, the bar goes up, and the only way an Indian stock can offer a better future return is for its price to fall today.

Then there's the dollar. A foreign investor measures returns in dollars. If the Nifty rises but the rupee falls by the same amount, they have earned nothing. So a strong dollar works against Indian assets twice: it erodes returns already earned, and it usually arrives with tighter money worldwide. That is why foreign selling, a rising dollar and rising US yields tend to show up together.

India carries what investors call a premium: it trades at richer valuations than most emerging markets because of its growth, its deep domestic market and its relatively clean governance. That premium is most fragile when US real yields are high.

The most exposed parts of the market are the ones foreigners own most of: large private banks, richly valued consumer and technology stories, and the biggest index names. The global chapter on the dollar and US rates explains how the premium is priced and why it can unwind so quickly.

sections.heading: Domestic flows: the buyer India built for itself
sections.html:
For most of the history of Indian markets, foreign investors were the marginal buyer. When they bought, the market rose. When they sold, it fell hard, because nobody at home had the money or the conviction to take the other side.

So what changed? In August 2015 the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, the giant retirement fund for salaried workers, bought shares for the first time in its history, through index funds tracking the Sensex and the Nifty. A slice of every provident fund contribution in the country now flows into the market each month. Systematic investment plans, or SIPs, where a fixed sum is debited from your bank account into a mutual fund every month, went from niche product to middle-class habit. Insurers and the National Pension System added their own steady stream. Then the pandemic sent a wave of first-time investors into brokerage accounts, and many of them stayed.

The jargon you will see everywhere is FII and DII. FIIs are foreign institutional investors, now officially foreign portfolio investors. DIIs are domestic institutional investors: mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and banks. When the daily data shows FIIs selling heavily and DIIs buying almost the same amount, that is domestic flows doing their job as a buffer.

Here's the catch. A buffer is not a floor. SIP money is sticky, but if the market goes nowhere for long enough, people pause their plans. And as the next chapter explains, Indian households have been borrowing more, so the cushion of spare savings behind those flows is thinner than it looks.

sections.heading: When the three variables gang up
sections.html:
The chart below is the whole argument in one picture: a decade of weekly data in three panels, Brent oil at the top, the US ten-year yield in the middle and the Nifty at the bottom. The shaded bands are the five stress episodes this course keeps coming back to.

[[fig:1]]

Read it from the bands outward. In each one, find the Nifty's dip in the bottom panel, then look up to see what oil and US yields were doing. The yuan devaluation of 2015 was a dollar and global-growth scare. The autumn of 2018 was oil climbing while a domestic credit accident unfolded. Covid was the odd one out: oil and yields both collapsed, because it was a crash in global demand, not a squeeze on supply. Ukraine in 2022 combined an oil spike with the fastest Fed hiking in decades. The band on the far right is the Iran war, with oil and US yields high at once.

Notice the bands are not equally deep in the bottom panel. That leads to a rough rule of thumb the rest of the course refines:

  • One adverse variable usually means a correction. A few sectors suffer, and the market recovers once the variable calms down.
  • Two at once usually means a proper drawdown. Oil and US rates squeezing together hit both earnings and the multiple, and foreign money tends to leave.
  • Domestic flows decide the depth. When home investors keep buying through the storm, the fall is shallower and shorter than foreign selling alone would suggest.

Look at 2022 through that lens. Oil spiked, the Fed hiked hard and foreigners sold at a record pace. Instead the Nifty fell through the first half and then recovered, because domestic institutions bought at a record pace too. Two adverse variables, one powerful buffer.

sections.heading: Two frameworks, and why you need both
sections.html:
If three variables explain most of the shared movement, why two frameworks? Because every shock has two halves: where it comes from, and how it travels once it reaches India. Think of weather and a house. The global framework is the forecast. The India framework is the state of your roof. A storm that barely bothers a well-built house can flood a leaky one.

Take an oil spike. Whether a barrel gets dearer is decided in the Gulf, in Moscow, in China's buying and in the shipping lanes. That is global. How much it hurts depends on how wide India's current account deficit already is, how much room the government has to cut fuel taxes, how many dollars the RBI holds and how stretched households are. That is domestic. The same barrel can be a nuisance one year and a crisis the next.

The India framework covers what is built at home: the national balance sheet (who saves, who borrows, how the gap with the world is funded), growth and which engine is accelerating, inflation and what the RBI reacts to, the RBI's three levers, the oil and rupee chain as India lives it, flows and positioning, fiscal policy and political economy, and a decade of Indian drawdowns and what caused each.

The global and geopolitical framework covers what arrives from outside: how the big economies reach India, the dollar and US rates, oil and the Gulf's chokepoints, China as price-setter and rival, Europe and Japan through energy and the carry trade, Russia and the sanctions era, conflict on India's borders, the technology and chip cycle, and the hot spots that could move markets next.

The synthesis joins the two into a regime view, works through the current oil shock end to end, and ends with a five-minute daily routine and its traps.

sections.heading: How to use this page
sections.html:
You do not have to read this front to back. Every chapter has the same shape. The hook and the short version give you the question and the conclusions in two minutes. The mechanism sections explain how the thing works, with a chart and a note on how to read it. The history cards tell the episodes that shaped how professionals think, the fastest way to build intuition. Where it stands now carries live readings: the words stay put while the numbers refresh from our daily data, and a late source is flagged rather than hidden. So what translates it into sector groups and ends with what would flip the call. It never names single stocks.

Each chapter also opens with a small box of indicators to track between visits. New to macro? Go in order. Otherwise start with the variable you understand least; most professionals have a blind spot, either the global plumbing of dollars and yields or the domestic plumbing of savings and flows. And if a crisis is unfolding, jump to the synthesis case study and follow its pointers back.

history_title: how the three variables took turns

history.title: The airlift, the oil bill and the empty vault
history.story:
In August 1990 Saddam Hussein's army rolled into Kuwait, and well over a hundred thousand Indians working in Kuwait and Iraq were stranded overnight. Over the next two months Air India and the Indian Air Force flew them home in hundreds of flights, an evacuation so large that Air India landed in the Guinness record books.

The human story hid an economic one. Those workers had been sending money home every month, and that stream of dollars stopped. At the same moment the war sent oil soaring, so India's import bill jumped just as its dollar income fell. Reserves drained fast, setting up the gold pledge, the devaluation and the reforms of the summer of 1991.
history.lesson: Oil plus a thin external buffer is India's oldest crisis recipe, and the remittance side of the ledger matters as much as the oil side.

history.title: A few sentences in Washington
history.story:
In May 2013 Ben Bernanke, then chairman of the Federal Reserve, told the US Congress that the Fed might slow its bond buying in the next few meetings. He did not raise rates or even decide anything. US bond yields jumped anyway, and money began pouring out of emerging markets.

India was among the hardest hit. Foreign funds dumped Indian bonds and the rupee slid all summer to a record low in late August. That month a Morgan Stanley analyst grouped India with Brazil, Indonesia, Turkey and South Africa as the Fragile Five, economies too dependent on skittish foreign money. The label stuck for years after the rupee recovered.
history.lesson: US rates matter most when India's external gap is wide, and a hint from the Fed can do more damage than an actual hike.

history.title: Black Monday, made in Beijing
history.story:
In August 2015 China's central bank surprised the world by devaluing the yuan, its biggest move against the dollar in about two decades. Markets read it as a sign that China was weaker than Beijing admitted, and would export its slowdown by making its goods cheaper everywhere.

Two weeks later, on a Monday that Chinese state media itself called Black Monday, Shanghai collapsed and the panic went global. The Sensex suffered its biggest single-day points fall up to that time and the rupee hit a two-year low. Nothing had changed in India's economy that morning. The shock came entirely through the dollar and global risk appetite.
history.lesson: A global dollar and growth scare can sink Indian stocks even on a quiet domestic day, so watch the outside variables every day.

history.title: A Friday afternoon in the bond market
history.story:
By the autumn of 2018 oil was at a four-year high and the rupee at record lows. Then the domestic credit system cracked. IL&FS, a giant infrastructure lender rated top-notch until shortly before, began defaulting in August and September.

On a Friday afternoon in late September, a mutual fund sold a block of short-term paper issued by the housing lender DHFL at a much higher yield than the market expected. Traders read it as distress, and DHFL's shares lost more than half their value in minutes before recovering part of the fall. Within days the government took over the IL&FS board and installed the banker Uday Kotak as chairman.
history.lesson: An outside shock that lands on a hidden domestic weakness does far more damage than either alone.

history.title: The lockdown generation
history.story:
In March 2020 the pandemic crashed markets worldwide, and the prime minister announced a national lockdown in an evening television address. The Nifty fell faster than at almost any time in its history. Then something unexpected happened. Stuck at home, with deposit rates falling and the market on sale, millions of Indians opened brokerage accounts for the first time, many on their phones.

The pace of new accounts nearly tripled compared with the year before, the market regulator's chairman, Ajay Tyagi, noted. Many of them started SIPs. A monthly, salary-linked flow into Indian shares became a mass habit.
history.lesson: A structural domestic buyer changes how deep sell-offs go, which is why domestic flows earned their place as the third variable.

history.title: All three at once
history.story:
In late February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine and Brent spiked to levels not seen since 2008. By June, with American inflation at multi-decade highs, Jerome Powell's Fed raised rates by its largest single step since 1994 and kept going. The dollar surged, and foreign investors pulled money out of Indian shares at a record pace for a calendar year.

On the old playbook this was a crash. Instead, domestic mutual funds and insurers bought at a record pace too, fuelled by SIP flows that kept rising month after month. The Nifty fell through the first half, then clawed back to end 2022 slightly higher, while most emerging markets finished in the red.
history.lesson: When all three variables move at once, the domestic buffer decides the outcome, so watch SIP flows as closely as oil and the Fed.

sowhat:
Two of the three variables are adverse and domestic flows are the buffer. That points to a clear pattern of sector pressure.

  • Prefer businesses whose profits rise with oil or a weaker rupee: upstream oil and gas producers, and exporters with dollar revenues such as IT services and pharmaceuticals, as long as global demand holds.
  • Be careful with heavy users of crude and its derivatives: airlines, paints, tyres, chemicals, and state-run fuel retailers when pump prices are held down.
  • Be careful with richly valued growth stocks and the names foreigners own most heavily, the first to feel high US real yields.
  • Watch the monthly mutual fund data. Rising SIP stoppages would be the earliest sign the buffer is thinning.

What would flip it: oil falling back and US yields easing would take two adverse variables off the table, and the most punished sectors usually lead the rebound. A sustained drop in domestic flows would make the setup far more dangerous.
